item.passage:
The screen door on the back porch had been dragging for two summers. It scraped a pale arc into the floorboards whenever someone came in from the yard, and instead of clapping shut it stopped an inch short of the frame and hung there, letting in moths.

"We could just buy a new one," Theo said. "The hardware store has aluminum ones for forty dollars. I looked."

His mother was already lifting the door off its hinges. She laid it flat across two sawhorses in the driveway and handed him a carpenter's square, a steel L with a perfect corner. "Check the corners first."

Theo set the square into one corner of the frame, then the next. At every corner a thin line of daylight opened between the steel and the wood, wide enough at the far end to slide a pencil into.

"It's racked," his mother said. "The whole frame has leaned, so the latch side hangs low. That's why it drags. The wood itself is fine." From a paper bag she took a length of thin steel cable, two brackets, and a small threaded barrel with a hook at each end. "This runs corner to corner, from the top on the hinge side down to the bottom on the latch side. You turn the barrel, the cable shortens, and it pulls the low corner back up."

Theo screwed the brackets in where she pointed and hooked the cable between them. He gripped the barrel and turned it. The cable went taut. He kept turning, and the line of daylight under the square narrowed and closed. He gave the barrel two more turns for good measure.

"Check it again," his mother said.

The daylight was back, along the other arm of the square this time. The corner that had hung too low now stood too high.

"Well, that's a new problem," Theo said.

His mother was grinning. "That's the old problem facing the other way." She loosened the barrel a half turn and stepped back. "Now let it sit a minute. Wood takes a while to settle."

They waited. Theo checked the corner, loosened the barrel a quarter turn, and waited again. It took four rounds before the steel lay flush against both edges of the frame, and by then the shade of the garage had crept across the driveway and over the sawhorses.

They carried the door back to the porch and hung it. Theo pulled it open and let go. It swung across without touching the boards and met the frame with a single flat clap, a sound he had not heard since he was twelve.

From the front room his grandmother called, "Who's home?"

"Just us," Theo called back. He looked down at the pale arc in the floorboards. It would take a long time to wear away, but nothing would add to it now.

Above our street the sky is never black.
It holds the color of a stove coil cooling,
an orange lid the streetlights push up
from below and the low clouds hand back.

My grandmother, who grew up
past the last bus stop of a smaller country,
looks up from the fire escape and says
the sky here has been painted over.

She tells me where the stars should be:
a road of them, thick as spilled flour,
running from the water tower to the bridge.
I squint and find one airplane, blinking,

and one steady point she says is a planet,
because it will not shimmer the way a star would.
That is all the sky can spare tonight:
a plane, a planet, and the tower's red light.

My brother pressed a sky onto my ceiling
the summer before he left for college,
plastic stars that drink the lamplight
and give it back for a few green minutes.

He put the Dipper over the closet door
and got it backward, my grandmother says;
on the real one the handle bends the other way.
I have kept it backward. It is his.

Each night I switch the lamp off and watch them fade,
the small ones first, the big ones holding on,
until the ceiling is only ceiling
and the window is that orange lid again.

She says the stars are all still up there,
every night, behind the glow,
the way the far bank of a river
is still there in a fog.

I believe her the way I believe
in the ocean from the middle of the city:
a thing I keep without having seen it.
Some night I will ride past the last stop and look up.

For now I leave the lamp on a little longer
before bed, to give the plastic stars
a little more to give back.

We adopted Juniper from a greyhound rescue group the winter I was thirteen. She was four years old and had spent most of those years at a racetrack, sleeping in a crate in a long kennel building and racing on a sand oval. The woman who drove her to our house stood in the driveway and read us a list of ordinary things Juniper had probably never seen: carpet, mirrors, glass doors, stairs.

I had imagined that rescuing a dog would feel like a single moment, the leash passing from one hand to another. Instead, on the first evening, Juniper stood at the bottom of our staircase for twenty minutes, looking up at it the way I might look at a ladder leaning against a cloud. Our bedrooms were upstairs. She had decided the staircase was a wall.

My father tried carrying her, all sixty-five pounds and four long legs of her, and she went so stiff halfway up that he turned around and carried her back down. My sister tried a trail of cheese. Juniper ate the cheese off the bottom step, stretched her long neck for the second, and reached the third by standing on her toes, all four feet still on the hall floor. That was as far as it went.

So I lay down on the stairs. I did it without much of a plan; I was tired, and the staircase carpet was the softest place in reach. I lay on my back with my head on the fourth step and my feet on the floor, and Juniper came over and put her nose against my ear. Then she set one front paw on the first step, beside my hip, to get closer.

For the next week and a half I did my homework on the staircase, sitting one step higher each evening. She followed a step at a time, lying with her chin on the step below mine, though she would not go past it. On the eleventh evening I sat on the top step, and she came up the last three in a rush, as though she wanted it over with, and stood in the upstairs hall looking around at a floor she had only ever heard us walking on.

Going down took another month.

People who hear the story usually say that we rescued her, and I suppose the paperwork agrees. But the day the van came was only the day she changed addresses. The rescuing, if that is the word, happened one step at a time, and most of it was done by a dog deciding that a staircase was a place where a person could lie down.

Anyone who looks closely at the older buildings of Ostley will eventually notice small figures cut into the stone: an arrow, a pair of crossed lines, a letter M with a bar through it, a shape like a three-legged stool. They appear on the town hall, on the piers of the railway bridge, and on the foundations of perhaps two dozen houses. Visitors often take them for decoration, or for some kind of secret sign. Their real purpose was more ordinary. They were a way of keeping accounts.

From the 1850s until 1894, the Ostley Granite Company paid its stonecutters by the piece. A cutter earned a set amount for each block he shaped, and each man had his own mark, registered in the company's book beside his name. He cut it into one face of every block he finished. At the end of each week a clerk walked the yard, counted the marks, and figured the wages.

The marks served a second purpose that the cutters liked less. A block that cracked on the wagon, or arrived at a building site a finger's width too short, could be traced to the man who had cut it, and the cost was taken from his pay. Because builders wanted plain walls, the marks were usually placed on a face that would be hidden once the stone was set, such as the back of a block or a side buried in mortar. The ones visible today are mostly on stones that were turned during building or used somewhere other than planned.

In 1894 the company's new owner, Edwin Mosse, changed to paying daily wages. He argued that piece rates rewarded speed over care, and that a foreman watching the yard could judge good work better than a clerk counting figures. Within a few years the marks had stopped appearing on new stone. Cutters who joined the company after 1894 seem never to have registered one.

Today the Ostley Historical Society keeps the old register, and its members use it to match marks to names. It is slow work. Some marks were reused when a cutter left and a new man took his place, so a single figure may stand for two people thirty years apart. When the railway bridge was taken apart for repairs in 1978, the backs of its stones were exposed for one summer, and members photographed more than four hundred marks before the piers were rebuilt. For many of the men in the register, those photographs are the only evidence of which stones they cut. A sign made so that a man could be paid, and if necessary fined, has become the record that he was there at all.

item.passage:
Plant a bean seed upside down, and the seedling will still sort itself out. Its root curves around and heads down into the soil; its shoot turns and climbs toward the surface. A houseplant left by a window does something similar, more slowly, leaning its stems toward the glass. Plants cannot walk toward what they need, but they can grow toward it, and to do that they must first sense which way is down and where the light is coming from.

Some of the first careful experiments on light were done around 1880 by Charles Darwin and his son Francis, using young grass seedlings. A grass seedling first pushes up a slender sheath, and when light comes from one side, the sheath bends toward it. The Darwins found that when they covered just the tip of the sheath with a tiny cap that blocked light, the seedling grew straight up, even though the part that normally bends, a little way below the tip, was still in the light. When they covered the lower part and left the tip bare, the seedling bent as usual. The tip, they concluded, was sensing the light, and some kind of signal was traveling down to the region that bent.

That signal is now known to involve a plant hormone called auxin, which encourages cells to stretch. Light-sensitive proteins in the shoot respond mainly to blue light. When light falls from one side, more auxin ends up on the shaded side of the stem, the cells there lengthen faster than the cells facing the light, and the stem curves toward the brighter side, much as a line of marchers wheels around a corner when those on the outside take longer steps.

Sensing gravity relies on a different detector. In a root, the job falls largely to a small group of cells in the root cap, the tip that pushes through the soil first. These cells contain dense grains of starch that sink to whichever side of the cell is lowest, much as sand settles in a jar of water. When a root is turned on its side, the grains settle against what used to be a side wall, auxin is shifted toward the new lower side, and the root bends until it is growing downward again. If the root cap is carefully removed, the root keeps growing but loses much of its ability to turn downward.

The starch grains are probably only part of the story, and some of the most interesting work now lies in the rest of it. Plants with a genetic change that leaves them unable to make this starch still turn their roots downward, though more slowly and less reliably. Some researchers think that the weight of a cell's whole contents, pressing on its outer layer, may supply a second signal. How the different signals are combined is still being worked out.

What is clear is that a seedling is constantly checking. Tip its pot onto its side, and within a few hours the shoot will usually begin to correct itself, bending until it points upward again.
